title: Design secrets, certificates and keys management
learningObjective: Recommend how to store and use secrets, certificates and encryption keys: Key Vault tiers, Managed HSM, access model, rotation and network isolation.
foundation: Passwords, connection strings, certificates and encryption keys must never live in code or config files.
Azure Key Vault stores them centrally. Apps read them with their managed identity, so nothing secret is written down.
If regulation demands dedicated hardware for keys, use Managed HSM.
engineer: Tiers: Key Vault Standard (secrets, certificates, software-protected keys); Key Vault Premium (adds HSM-protected keys in multi-tenant HSMs); Managed HSM (single-tenant HSM pool, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated, you control the security domain) for the strictest key custody needs.

Access: use the Azure RBAC permission model (Key Vault Secrets User, Crypto Service Encryption User, Key Vault Administrator) rather than legacy access policies; give apps managed identities; separate the management plane (create vaults) from the data plane (read secrets).

Protection: soft delete (always on, 7–90 days) and purge protection (cannot be turned off once enabled; required for customer-managed keys in many services); private endpoints and disabled public network access; logging with diagnostic settings; Defender for Key Vault.

Lifecycle: key rotation policies, certificate auto-renewal with integrated CAs, Event Grid notifications for near-expiry. Design one vault per application per environment per region to limit blast radius and throttling. App settings in App Service and Functions can use Key Vault references; App Configuration holds non-secret settings and references Key Vault for secrets.

animation.caption: Choose Key Vault Standard, Premium, Managed HSM or App Configuration.

example.title: Customer-managed keys for a payments platform
body: Storage and SQL use customer-managed keys from Key Vault Premium with purge protection and a yearly rotation policy. Each app and environment has its own vault, reached through private endpoints.
The card-tokenisation service, which must meet single-tenant HSM requirements, uses Managed HSM.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription; most design reviews need only Reader access
permissions: Reader to review existing resources; Contributor or Owner to build the design
limits: Check service limits and regional availability for each component
portal: Create a resource > Key Vault: pricing tier, soft delete days, purge protection, permission model = Azure RBAC, Networking = private endpoint.
configuration.cli:
az keyvault create -g rg-app -n kv-orders-prod-weu --sku premium --enable-purge-protection true --enable-rbac-authorization true --public-network-access Disabled
az role assignment create --assignee <identity-principal-id> --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --scope <vault-id>

lab.objective: Choose where secrets, keys and settings belong.
expected: Premium for HSM-backed keys; Managed HSM for single-tenant
failureScenarios: Storing feature flags in Key Vault
Sharing one vault across every app and environment
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: Enabling customer-managed keys on storage fails.
troubleshooting.cause: Purge protection or soft delete not enabled on the vault, or the storage identity lacks key permissions.
troubleshooting.fix: Enable purge protection and grant Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User.

troubleshooting.symptom: Apps get HTTP 429 from Key Vault at startup.
troubleshooting.cause: Too many reads against one vault.
troubleshooting.fix: Cache secrets in the app and split vaults per app.

comparisons.service: Key Vault Premium vs Managed HSM
comparisons.difference: Premium: HSM-backed keys in a multi-tenant service. Managed HSM: dedicated single-tenant HSM pool, you own the security domain.
Key Vault for secrets; App Configuration for settings and feature flags.

misconceptions.reality: It is always on for new vaults.

misconceptions.myth: Access policies and RBAC are the same.
misconceptions.reality: RBAC is the recommended model, with fine-grained, scope-based roles.

architectureDecisions: Vault per app, per environment, per region.
Purge protection and private endpoints for production.

walkthrough.subtitle: Keep every secret, certificate and key in one safe place that apps can reach without passwords.
learn: Key Vault tiers and Managed HSM
Access with managed identities and RBAC
Protection: soft delete, purge protection, private access
Rotation and one vault per app

steps.label: Problem
steps.title: A connection string was committed to Git
body: Secrets in code leak. Design a place where secrets live and a way for apps to read them without another secret.

steps.label: Tiers
steps.title: Pick the vault
body: Key Vault Standard: secrets, certificates and software keys. Premium: adds keys protected by hardware security modules. Managed HSM: your own single-tenant HSM pool for the strictest rules.

steps.label: Access
steps.title: Managed identity + RBAC
body: The app's managed identity gets the Key Vault Secrets User role on its vault. No password anywhere.

steps.label: Protect
steps.title: Soft delete, purge protection, private endpoint
body: Soft delete keeps deleted items for 7–90 days; purge protection stops anyone destroying them early. A private endpoint keeps the vault off the internet.

callout.text: Purge protection cannot be turned off once enabled — that is the point.

steps.label: Lifecycle
steps.title: Rotate, and keep settings separate
body: Rotation policies renew keys and certificates automatically. Use one vault per app, environment and region. Non-secret settings and feature flags go in App Configuration, which can reference Key Vault.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Secrets design
recap: Soft delete + purge protection + private endpoint

handsOn.title: Store a secret in Key Vault and read it with RBAC
handsOn.cost: Low. Key Vault Standard charges per 10,000 operations; this lab uses a handful (well under one US cent).
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription. Work in a resource group called rg-az305-lab.
If rg-az305-lab does not exist yet: Resource groups > Create > name rg-az305-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.

steps.do: Create a vault with the Azure RBAC permission model (use a unique name).
steps.see: The vault's JSON, with enableRbacAuthorization true and enableSoftDelete true.
steps.tip: Purge protection is left off so the lab can be cleaned up today. Turn it on for production.
steps.code: KV=kv-az305-$RANDOM; az keyvault create -g rg-az305-lab -n $KV --enable-rbac-authorization true; echo $KV

steps.do: Try to add a secret right away.
steps.see: An error: you are not authorized.
steps.tip: Owner manages the vault (control plane) but has no data-plane role yet.

steps.do: Give yourself the Key Vault Secrets Officer role on the vault, wait a minute, then retry.
steps.code:
az role assignment create --assignee $(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv) --role "Key Vault Secrets Officer" --scope $(az keyvault show -n $KV --query id -o tsv)
sleep 60
az keyvault secret set --vault-name $KV -n db-password --value 'Lab-Only-123!'
az keyvault secret show --vault-name $KV -n db-password --query value -o tsv

steps.see: Soft-delete retention days and the purge protection setting.

check: You saw RBAC block access until a data-plane role was assigned.
cleanup: Delete the resource group (the vault becomes soft-deleted).
Optional: Key vaults > Manage deleted vaults > Purge, to free the name.
